text: We're closing out Chapter 2 with a word that ties everything you've learned together: predicate. You've been writing predicates this entire chapter without necessarily calling them that.

A predicate is simply any expression that evaluates to true, false, or unknown — that last one being the special result NULL comparisons produce, from Lesson 16. In plain terms, a predicate is how SQL Server actually filters data. List price greater than 100 — that whole condition is the predicate.

Look back over this chapter, and every single filtering tool you learned is really just a different flavor of predicate. A plain comparison. AND, OR, and NOT combining several together. LIKE for pattern matching. IN and BETWEEN for lists and ranges. IS NULL for checking absence. Six different shapes, one underlying concept.

And predicates aren't only for WHERE. You already used one back in Chapter 1 — every WHEN clause inside a searched CASE is a predicate too. Later, in Chapter 3, the condition after JOIN and ON is a predicate. In Chapter 4, HAVING filters using a predicate as well. Once you see predicates as one unifying idea, a lot of T-SQL clicks into place.

That closes out Chapter 2. You can filter, combine conditions, match patterns, check ranges and lists, handle NULL, sort, and limit your results. Chapter 3 builds directly on all of it: combining data from multiple tables with joins — and yes, every join condition you write is, unsurprisingly, a predicate too. See you there.
